rationale.test: Give managers an orientation task and a case-investigation task, then give processors a direct lookup task using the same records. Observe where they look first, whether they misread totals as trends, and whether the cards help explain their decision. Compare task completion and wrong turns with the work-queue direction. Change the recommendation if managers cannot use the metrics to answer a real question or processors consistently bypass them.
rationale.bestFor: A lending manager doing a periodic portfolio review: first establish scale and readiness, then investigate a particular application or stage. This direction assumes orientation is a meaningful part of the visit.
rationale.poorFit: I would reject this as the default if observed sessions start with search and users routinely skip the summaries. I would also reject any claim that it is a performance dashboard until the design has meaningful comparisons or targets; a large number without context is not an insight.
rationale.summary: Understand portfolio health before investigating an individual loan.
rationale.tradeoff: Every repeat visit pays the vertical cost of the metric row before reaching records. The information is also aggregate, so a processor may have to mentally separate team totals from their own work. This is a poor bargain if most visits are direct case lookups.

decisions.title: Summary first, evidence directly below
decisions.explanation: The metric row establishes a small set of questions before the user encounters eight detailed records. Keeping the table immediately below supports a summary-to-evidence sequence without sending the user elsewhere. But the current metrics do not filter the table, so they should read as summaries rather than imply clickable drill-down. A later interaction could make that transition explicit, provided the selected filter is visible.

decisions.title: Give the three metrics distinct meanings
decisions.explanation: Value, volume and readiness describe different dimensions of the portfolio. Equal-sized cards make them easy to scan as a set, but equal styling also asserts equal importance. I would ask which decision each metric supports before keeping that equality. If readiness drives the daily meeting, it deserves priority; if total value is merely decorative, it should lose prominence rather than survive because dashboards traditionally have three cards.

decisions.title: Separate creation from investigation
decisions.explanation: Placing New application beside the heading makes it a stable, page-level action. It no longer interrupts the scan from summaries into records, and it is less likely to be mistaken for an action on the filtered table. The strong button still competes with the data for attention. If creation is rare for this audience, I would reduce its visual weight rather than assume every page needs a dominant primary action.

rationale.assumption: We have portfolio totals and stage labels, but no research showing which decisions managers actually make here. The three metrics are counts or totals, not health indicators by themselves: eight applications could be healthy or problematic depending on age, staffing and expectations.
rationale.hypothesis: This design gives the first screenful to three management questions: how much work exists, how much value it represents, and how much is near completion. The table is the explanation layer beneath that summary. That is a deliberate priority choice: understand the portfolio before acting on a case.

annotations.text: Volume, value and readiness establish the portfolio picture before the user scans individual cases.
annotations.title: Orient before investigating

annotations.text: A page-level action leaves the summaries-to-records reading path uninterrupted.
annotations.title: Creation stays separate

annotations.text: Frequent processors must pass the metric row on every visit. Prefer the work queue if lookup dominates.

rationale.test: Ask processors to find a known loan, locate work owned by a colleague, and explain what they would do next. Use realistic long names and the smallest common viewport. Record filter mistakes, row-reading errors and attempts to find urgency information that is not present. Prefer this direction only if it improves lookup without making comparison harder; reconsider the rail if users never refer to it.
rationale.bestFor: A processor returning repeatedly to locate a known loan or narrow work by owner and stage. The design favors getting into a record quickly while keeping team-level context available at the side.
rationale.poorFit: I would reject the side rail if realistic records cause wrapping or horizontal scrolling at the team’s normal viewport. I would also reject this as an actionable priority queue if users need to know what is urgent: the available fields cannot justify an urgency order or a recommended next case.
rationale.summary: Put finding and progressing a loan ahead of portfolio reporting.
rationale.tradeoff: The right rail takes width from a six-column table. That can increase wrapping and slow row scanning, especially with long names or a smaller laptop viewport. Keeping every metric visible may be less valuable than giving the main task more space.

decisions.title: Promote the work surface, not just the search box
decisions.explanation: Moving the whole table up preserves the relationship between search, filters and their results. It is more coherent than placing a prominent search field elsewhere and making the user look away to understand its effect. The hypothesis is that repeated visits involve record retrieval. If users instead need to decide which kind of work to do, this layout makes the tools easy to find but leaves the more important decision unsupported.

decisions.title: Read identity, state and responsibility together
decisions.explanation: Borrower, status and owner form a practical triage cluster: which case is this, where is it in the process, and who is responsible? Amount and purpose remain available but follow that cluster. This order is justified only for workflow-oriented tasks. A financial reviewer comparing exposure may need amount earlier, so column priority should follow the role’s decisions rather than a universal definition of a good table.

decisions.title: Treat the metric rail as expendable context
decisions.explanation: The vertical rail preserves portfolio awareness without pushing records lower. Its cost is paid in table width, not empty space. I would test it with long borrower and owner names and remove or collapse it before compromising readable rows. Persistent visibility is not automatically helpful: secondary information should earn the space it takes from the primary task.

rationale.assumption: The source supports lookup and filtering; it does not identify the next best action, deadlines or blocked work. Calling this a work queue describes its layout, not a proven prioritization system. We still need to establish whether processors know what they are looking for or arrive needing guidance.
rationale.hypothesis: This direction treats the table as the work surface rather than as supporting evidence for a dashboard. Moving summaries into a side rail brings search, stage filters and records higher on the page. Reordering columns puts assignment and process state alongside identity—the information a processor is likely to need before financial detail.

annotations.text: Owner and status sit beside borrower identity, so processors can read assignment without scanning the whole row.
annotations.title: Scan responsibility early

annotations.text: Search, filters and their results start higher on the page. This serves repeat lookup, not portfolio reporting.
annotations.title: Records come first

annotations.text: Totals stay visible, but consume table width. Remove this rail if real names wrap or columns become cramped.
annotations.title: Cost: narrower records

recommendation.reason: Search, assignment and stage take priority over totals.
recommendation.condition: Lookup is the main task and the metric rail leaves enough table width.

rationale.test: In a team review, ask participants to describe the distribution and identify a handoff worth discussing, then ask them to compare loan amounts across stages. Observe whether the board improves a shared explanation or simply looks more engaging. Deliberately ask what the counts cannot tell them. Reject bottleneck claims unsupported by age and capacity, and prefer the table direction if comparison tasks dominate.
rationale.bestFor: A team reviewing handoffs or sharing an understanding of the pipeline. The stages provide a common vocabulary for the conversation; the detailed table remains available for exact lookup and comparison.
rationale.poorFit: I would reject this as the default for high-volume portfolios unless the board has a clear strategy for density and retrieval. I would also avoid it if stakeholders interpret a larger column as a bottleneck or expect drag-and-drop to change a loan’s state; neither conclusion is supported by this implementation.
rationale.summary: Discuss where work sits before comparing individual loan details.
rationale.tradeoff: Cards consume more vertical space and are weaker than aligned table columns for comparing amounts, owners or purposes across all records. The table below restores that capability at the cost of a longer page and duplicated information.

decisions.title: Make stage membership visible without mental sorting
decisions.explanation: Separate labeled columns group records spatially, so the team does not have to scan every status chip and hold the groups in memory. This supports a handoff conversation. It also places the burden on the stage model: ambiguous or overlapping stages would make the organization misleading. I would validate those definitions with the people doing the work before polishing the board.

decisions.title: Use counts to describe distribution, not severity
decisions.explanation: Counts in the column headings summarize the records visibly contained in each stage. Neutral styling avoids inventing red or green judgments. A count of three is not worse than two without information about capacity, age or normal throughput. If the product needs to expose bottlenecks, I would first obtain those missing measures instead of asking visual emphasis to imply a conclusion the data cannot support.

decisions.title: Keep a list for the tasks a board handles poorly
decisions.explanation: The table below retains search, filters and aligned values for exact comparison. That makes the tradeoff visible rather than pretending the board replaces every function. In a production design, a Board/List switch might avoid duplicated content and scrolling. I would only add it if both views serve recurring tasks and preserve filter state, so switching does not force users to reconstruct their context.

rationale.assumption: The supplied records support a 3 / 2 / 3 distribution across stages. They contain no time in stage, service targets or capacity data. The design therefore shows where work is, not where it is stuck, and assumes the named stages match the team’s actual handoff process.
rationale.hypothesis: This direction changes the organizing principle from one list of records to three process stages. People can see the distribution without repeatedly reading the status column and mentally grouping rows. That externalizes one useful operation, but it does not establish whether any stage is performing well.
